client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to get my head straight. Every time I sit down to study, I end up just staring at the page thinking about him, and then I feel guilty for not studying, which makes everything worse. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me actually open my textbooks, you know?
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandfather — grieving while facing exams is an incredibly heavy burden to carry, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps drifting to him rather than your textbooks. What you're describing — that cycle of distraction, then guilt, then more distraction — is actually a very common and understandable response to grief, not a sign that something is wrong with you. I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, and I think that's worth honoring — so I'm curious, when you imagine sitting down to study tonight, what's the very first thought that tends to show up in your mind?

client: Honestly, the first thought that shows up is something like... "what's the point?" Like, my grandfather always asked me how school was going, and now there's no one to tell when I do well. It just feels hollow, and then I feel guilty for even thinking that way instead of just pushing through like I'm supposed to.
therapist: That thought — "what's the point?" — makes so much sense when you realize that part of what motivated you was sharing your success with someone who genuinely cared, and that's a real and meaningful loss, not a weakness or an excuse. I also want to gently push back on that word "supposed to" — who decided that grief has a timeline, and that you should just be pushing through right now? It might be worth exploring whether your grandfather, knowing how much he cared about your school life, would actually want you to feel guilty for missing him in this very tender way.

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly, because I know the answer — he would hate seeing me beat myself up like this. But it's easier to say that than to actually feel it, you know? Like, my brain understands it, but there's still this voice that says I'm just making excuses for falling behind.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — that gap between *knowing* something and truly *feeling* it is at the heart of so much of our struggle, and it doesn't mean you're failing or making excuses, it means you're human and grieving. That critical inner voice calling everything an "excuse" sounds like it's trying to protect you by keeping you on track, but it might actually be making it harder to do the very thing it wants. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you in exactly your situation, losing someone important right before exams, would you tell them they were just making excuses?

client: I mean... no, obviously I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them it makes complete sense that they're struggling, that grief doesn't just pause for exams. But it feels different when it's me — like I don't deserve the same kind of understanding I'd give someone else, and I don't really know why that is.
therapist: What you just noticed — that you freely offer compassion to others but feel you don't deserve it yourself — is such an honest and courageous insight, and it's actually one of the most common patterns I see in people who care deeply and hold themselves to high standards. That difference in treatment isn't a truth about your worth; it's a habit of thinking that can gently be questioned and changed over time. I'm curious — what do you think it would feel like, even just for today, to try treating yourself as you would that friend — not as a grand gesture, but in one small, concrete way?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it, but there's this immediate voice that says "that's just something therapists are supposed to tell people." Like, intellectually I can follow the logic, but emotionally it feels like trying to put on clothes that belong to someone else. And honestly, I'm not even sure what treating myself like a friend would look like in practice, because I've been hard on myself for so long that I don't really know what the alternative feels like.
therapist: That skepticism you're feeling is actually really healthy and worth respecting — you're not just going to accept something because it sounds nice, and that tells me you want something real, not just reassuring words. The "clothes that don't fit" image you used is actually perfect, because self-compassion genuinely does feel awkward and foreign at first when you're not used to it, almost like a muscle you haven't used in a long time. So rather than trying to *feel* it right away, I wonder if we could just start with something tiny and behavioral — like, what would you physically *do* differently in the next hour if you were caring for a grieving friend who also had exams, rather than trying to force yourself to feel a certain way about it?

client: I mean, I guess if it were a friend I'd probably tell them to take a break, maybe get some water or food, not just sit there staring at their notes feeling terrible about themselves. But when I try to apply that to me it just feels... performative, like I'm going through the motions without actually believing I deserve it. And honestly there's this voice in the back of my head saying if I go easy on myself I'll just fall apart completely and fail everything.
therapist: That fear — "if I stop being hard on myself, everything will collapse" — is actually worth examining, because it's doing a lot of work in keeping you stuck; it's essentially arguing that your self-criticism is the only thing holding you together, when in reality it might be the very thing draining the energy you need to study. And the "performative" feeling makes complete sense at first, because doing something kind for yourself before you *believe* you deserve it isn't fake — it's actually how the belief slowly gets built, through small actions that gradually become evidence. I'm curious, has there ever been a time in your life when being a little gentler with yourself actually helped you function *better*, even briefly — or does your mind insist that's never happened?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my instinct is to say no, being gentle with myself has never helped. But actually... there was this one time during my first year when I was completely burned out and I just kind of gave myself a weekend off, no studying, no guilt-tripping myself, and I came back on Monday feeling sharper than I had in weeks. I almost forgot about that, which is kind of strange when I think about it now.
therapist: That memory is so important, and the fact that your mind almost buried it makes complete sense — when we're in a self-critical pattern, our brain tends to filter out evidence that contradicts it, which is why it felt strange to remember. You just found real, lived proof from your own life that rest and self-compassion didn't make you fall apart — they actually helped you come back stronger. I'm wondering, what feels different about that weekend you gave yourself permission to rest, compared to what you're allowing yourself right now?

client: I guess... that weekend felt different because I didn't have anyone watching or judging me. I was alone, and somehow that made it feel safer to just stop for a bit without feeling like I was letting someone down. But right now, even when I'm physically alone, it's like I've internalized all those voices and I'm judging myself harder than anyone else ever could.
therapist: What you just described — realizing that you've become your own harshest judge, stricter than anyone external ever was — is a genuinely profound insight, and it takes real self-awareness to see that so clearly. That internalized voice likely developed for good reasons, maybe to protect you or to meet expectations that mattered, but it sounds like it's now working overtime in a moment when you actually need gentleness most. I'm curious — if you could identify whose voice that inner critic most sounds like, or where it first came from, does anyone or anything come to mind?

client: Honestly, when you ask whose voice it is... my dad's face comes to mind almost immediately, which is uncomfortable to admit. He wasn't cruel or anything, but nothing was ever quite good enough — there was always a "but you could have done better" after every achievement. I guess I just... absorbed that standard and made it my own, and now I can't seem to turn it off even when he's not around.
therapist: That took real courage to name, and the discomfort you feel saying it out loud actually speaks to how much you've carried this quietly for a long time. What's striking is that you've essentially become so good at anticipating that "but you could have done better" that you now deliver it to yourself before anyone else can — it became a way of protecting yourself, but it's now a voice that never lets you rest, even in grief. I'm gently wondering, do you think your grandfather — the person you're missing right now, the one who asked about your school life — did he make you feel like it was never quite enough, or did he offer you something different?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly... no, he wasn't like that at all. He was one of the only people who just seemed genuinely happy to see me, no conditions attached, no scorecard. And I think that's part of why losing him hurts so much — like, that voice that says "not enough" was never his, it came from somewhere else, and now he's gone and I can't... I don't know, it's like I lost the one place where I didn't have to earn anything.
therapist: What you just said is so tender and so important — your grandfather wasn't just a person you loved, he was a living reminder that you are enough simply as you are, and losing him means losing that safe place where the "not enough" voice went quiet. That's a profound and specific grief, and it makes complete sense that studying feels hollow right now, because part of what made achievement feel meaningful was being able to bring it to someone who celebrated *you*, not just your performance. I'm wondering — is there any way to honor that part of him, that unconditional presence he offered you, by trying to offer even a small piece of that same acceptance to yourself right now, almost as a way of keeping something of him alive?
